newsitem.title: UK: Britain orders major review of live animal exports.
newsitem.headline: Britain orders major review of live animal exports.

text.p: Britain said on Tuesday it has ordered a major review of rules on the export of live animals to the continent, a subject that has triggered widespread protests.
Elliot Morley, agriculture minister in the new Labour government, said the move reflected public concern about the welfare of the animals and criticism about the current arrangements.
"Where animals are exported live, the public must have full confidence that the strictest possible welfare rules are being applied to this trade," he said in a statement.
"Accordingly we have ordered an urgent review of the arrangements for ensuring that animals are rested, fed, watered and cleared as fit prior to export in accordance with the law."
Morley said the government also planned to implement new European Union rules on animal transit, including limits on journey time, that were agreed in 1995.
"We will not compromise on these standards," he promised.
Animals rights groups, long concerned about the treatment during export, welcomed the move.
"We are very, very pleased," Peter Stevens of Campassion in World Farming (CWF) said.

"Ideally we want to see live export banned because we believe it is cruel but this announcement represents a major shift for the government. Basically they are saying they are not going to ban the trade but they are encouraging a major shift away from live exports towards meat."
He said the move should also lead to big improvements in the way animals are exported from this country.
CWF called for a public boycott of ferry giant P&O Steam and Navigation Co last month in protest against its policy to carry live animals to continental slaughterhouses.
It claimed the animals were destined for cruel culling procedures overseas and suffered distress from the sea journey.
During the past two years animal activists have carried out huge demonstrations which attracted large support from ordinary Britons disgusted by trade in live animals.

Several British docks were hit by violent demonstrations by animal rights activists in 1995 and one woman protester was killed when she was crushed by a truck carrying calves to be loaded on to a cargo plane.
